name: Availability cascade
statement: An expressed perception gains plausibility through its own repetition in public, as people copy the beliefs of others and hide their doubts, until the consensus drives costly law.
meaning: Kuran and Sunstein put two known mechanisms together. An informational cascade runs when people with little private knowledge treat the apparent beliefs of others as evidence, so each new endorsement raises the next person's estimate. A reputational cascade runs on approval rather than evidence. People voice the view that will not get them criticised, and the missing dissent removes what would have slowed the process. Joined, and fed by the availability heuristic, the two make a perception more available in public discourse, and that availability is then read as support for it. Activists who work to start such a process are called availability entrepreneurs. The claim is about the compound, not about any of its parts. The availability heuristic has its own entry here, and its evidence does not carry over.

origin.who: Timur Kuran and Cass R. Sunstein
origin.note: The article ran in volume 51, issue 4, pages 683 to 768, and coins the term. Its own footnote 3 places the informational half in a literature headed by Banerjee and by Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch, and the reputational half in one headed by Akerlof and by Kuran's earlier papers on preference falsification. The purpose is a policy argument rather than a finding. The article proposes peer review, cost-benefit analysis, a trusted government risk website and product disparagement law as brakes on cascades.

evidence: The article contains no data. It is eighty-six pages of argument, one table and three narrated cases, and the cases are reconstructions from published accounts rather than measurements. Love Canal gets the longest treatment, and its opening footnote names two Lois Gibbs memoirs and Aaron Wildavsky's But Is It True? as the sources drawn on primarily, with page citations omitted for readability. Alar rests on Wildavsky again. TWA Flight 800 rests on a 1997 law review article by Robert Hahn. The brief for this entry named the Times Beach dioxin case as the third example. It is not one, and dioxin appears in the article only inside the Love Canal narrative. The authors are explicit about what the cases are for. Footnote 101 says the examples were chosen because the data "nicely illustrate the phenomenon of regulatory action prompted by availability cascades rather than sound evidence", and that "nothing turns on the selected examples". A reader who thinks the science justified a given response is told the quarrel is with one interpretation and not with the argument. Footnote 18 makes the point as a joke: in convincing readers of the availability heuristic's significance the authors are exploiting the readers' reliance on it, and they "plead guilty". The conclusion lists seven claims the article has "tried to substantiate". Each is a proposition about mechanism, and none is attached to a measurement. The one table, of risk traits that make a hazard less acceptable, lists heavy media coverage among them and cites the psychometric risk literature generally rather than a study per row.

replication.headline: No study testing the availability cascade was located. The closest evidence tests its two halves separately, in settings with no risk, no regulator and no press.
replication.detail: The informational half has a laboratory literature. Anderson and Holt paid 72 University of Virginia undergraduates $2 for each correct prediction to say in sequence which of two urns a private draw came from. Cascades formed in 87 of the 122 periods in which they were possible. Reverse cascades, where an early run of unrepresentative draws starts a chain of wrong guesses that later draws do not break, were about half as common as correct ones. Subjects ignored the Bayesian inference and followed their own draw in 26 percent of the cases where the two conflicted, a figure from the symmetric sessions. The 87 of 122 is the twelve-session total; the symmetric sessions alone give 41 of 56 and the asymmetric 46 of 66. Goeree, Palfrey, Rogers and McKelvey then ran much longer sequences and found the cascades ephemeral. They form, collapse and re-form, a reversal is usually self-correcting in that the cascade switches to the right state, and the estimates show subjects overweighting their private information. The reputational half has field evidence. Bursztyn, Gonzalez and Yanagizawa-Drott ran sessions with 500 married Saudi men aged 18 to 35 in Riyadh. Eighty-seven percent privately agreed that women should be allowed to work outside the home, and about three-quarters underestimated how many of the other men in their own session agreed. Telling half of them the true count raised paid sign-up to a women's job-matching service by 9 percentage points from a base of 23 percent. Three to five months later their wives were 10 percentage points more likely to have applied for a job outside the home, from a base of 6 percent. Hale combined a nationally representative panel spanning Russia's post-Crimea rally with a list experiment and concluded that three quarters of those who rallied to Putin were dissembling to some degree, and that the rally developed as a rapid cascade. Neither literature involves a risk judgement or a news cycle. The one study located that tracks a real scare as it runs is Frewer, Miles and Marsh, who measured attitudes before, during and after the surge in British reporting on genetically modified food in spring 1999. Risk perceptions rose and fell with the coverage, perceived benefit stayed depressed afterwards, and trust in regulators did not move. That study tests the social amplification of risk framework, which is a different and earlier proposal.

limits: Nothing above tests the composite claim, and it is not obvious what a test would look like. The cascade predicts the same public record as a genuine discovery: rising coverage, converging opinion, regulation. Telling them apart needs an independent verdict on the underlying risk, which is what the disputes are about. Searching covered Crossref by bibliographic query, Semantic Scholar's citation list for the article, PubMed, and general web search pairing the term with experiment, replication and empirical test. The article is cited widely and the citing work applies the term rather than testing it. Several things could not be read. Combs and Slovic's 1979 content analysis, the usual citation for a correlation between newspaper coverage of causes of death and judged frequency, is paywalled, so the correlations quoted from it elsewhere are not repeated here. Wahlberg and Sjoberg's review of media and risk perception is paywalled. No sample size for the Frewer study appears in any abstract obtainable. Wildavsky's book and the Gibbs memoirs, which carry the article's factual account, were not obtained, so the Love Canal and Alar narratives are reported as the article gives them. On the transmission step the whole argument rests on, the risk-perception literature is cooler than the article suggests. Sjoberg's 2000 review reports that heuristics and biases, mainly availability, account for only a minor portion of risk perception, that media content has not been clearly implicated in it, and that the psychometric model, the leading contender in the field, explains only around 20 percent of the variance in raw data. Pachur's 2024 reanalysis found that media coverage overrepresents dramatic causes of death in every dataset, while the matching distortion in people's frequency judgements shows up only in the 1978 study, and is absent once the datasets are aggregated. That paper is treated at length in this site's availability heuristic entry.
misreadings: The cascade is not the availability heuristic. The heuristic is a claim about one person's judgement, and the cascade is a claim about what happens when many such judgements feed each other. The article's own conclusion says the heuristic standing by itself leaves important gaps, so evidence for the first is not evidence for the second. The term is now used as a verdict on beliefs a writer rejects, and the article does not support that use. It states that a cascade reshaping public discourse may be socially beneficial and can draw overdue attention to neglected problems, and that how much the distortions matter in any particular context is an empirical matter. The Alar case is the weakest of the three as it is usually retold. Kuran and Sunstein report the EPA's revised estimate of one child in 250,000 developing cancer, call it a nontrivial risk, and then quote Wildavsky's account of a United Nations panel finding even that figure too high. The EPA announcement of 7 November 1989 approved Uniroyal's voluntary cancellation of all food uses of daminozide, on the ground that its breakdown product UDMH causes tumours in laboratory animals and that lifetime dietary exposure may result in an unacceptable risk to public health. Elliott Negin argued in Columbia Journalism Review in 1996 that reviews completed after the broadcast, including one by Uniroyal, confirmed the studies the campaigners had relied on. The response was disproportionate on the article's own numbers. It was not about nothing. Love Canal is the better case, and its strongest evidence arrived ten years after the article. Gensburg and colleagues followed 5,052 former residents through the New York State Cancer Registry from 1979 to 1996 and found 304 cancers. All sites combined gave a standardised incidence ratio of 0.95 against New York State, on a 95 percent interval of 0.83 to 1.05. Bladder and kidney cancers were raised, at 1.44 and 1.48, on intervals that include 1.00. The authors write that the role of exposure to the landfill is unclear and that further surveillance is warranted.

sources.text: Kuran, T., & Sunstein, C. R. (1999). Availability cascades and risk regulation. Stanford Law Review, 51(4), 683-768. Full text read from the author's copy linked here; the DOI resolves to the JSTOR record.

Anderson, L. R., & Holt, C. A. (1997). Information cascades in the laboratory. American Economic Review, 87(5), 847-862. Full text read; source of the 72 subjects, the 87 of 122 periods, and the 26 percent deviation rate.

Goeree, J. K., Palfrey, T. R., Rogers, B. W., & McKelvey, R. D. (2007). Self-correcting information cascades. Review of Economic Studies, 74(3), 733-762. Read as abstract; finds cascades ephemeral in long sequences and reversals usually self-correcting.

Bursztyn, L., Gonzalez, A. L., & Yanagizawa-Drott, D. (2020). Misperceived social norms: Women working outside the home in Saudi Arabia. American Economic Review, 110(10), 2997-3029. Full text read for the 87 percent, the sign-up effect and the follow-up outcomes.

Hale, H. E. (2022). Authoritarian rallying as reputational cascade? Evidence from Putin's popularity surge after Crimea. American Political Science Review, 116(2), 580-594. Abstract read for the three-quarters figure.

Frewer, L. J., Miles, S., & Marsh, R. (2002). The media and genetically modified foods: Evidence in support of social amplification of risk. Risk Analysis, 22(4), 701-711. Abstract read; sample sizes not obtainable.

Kasperson, R. E., Renn, O., Slovic, P., Brown, H. S., Emel, J., Goble, R., Kasperson, J. X., & Ratick, S. (1988). The social amplification of risk: A conceptual framework. Risk Analysis, 8(2), 177-187. Cited for the framework the Frewer study tests; not read in full.

Sjoberg, L. (2000). Factors in risk perception. Risk Analysis, 20(1), 1-12. Abstract read in full; source of the 20 percent of variance and of the statement that media content has not been clearly implicated in risk perception.
Pachur, T. (2024). The perception of dramatic risks: Biased media, but unbiased minds. Cognition, 246, 105736. Abstract read in full; reanalysis of Lichtenstein et al. and its replications.

Gensburg, L. J., Pantea, C., Kielb, C., Fitzgerald, E., Stark, A., & Kim, N. (2009). Cancer incidence among former Love Canal residents. Environmental Health Perspectives, 117(8), 1265-1271. Abstract read in full for the cohort, the standardised incidence ratios and the conclusion.
US Environmental Protection Agency (1989). Daminozide (Alar) pesticide canceled for food uses. Press release, 7 November 1989. Read in full.
Negin, E. (1996). The Alar 'scare' was for real. Columbia Journalism Review, September/October 1996. Read as reprinted by PBS; disputes the standard retelling of the Alar episode.

Wahlberg, A. A. F., & Sjoberg, L. (2000). Risk perception and the media. Journal of Risk Research, 3(1), 31-50. Named here because it is the standing review of the question; it is paywalled and was not read.

Combs, B., & Slovic, P. (1979). Newspaper coverage of causes of death. Journalism Quarterly, 56(4), 837-849. Named here because it is the usual citation for the media-to-judgement correlation; it is paywalled and was not read, so no figure from it appears above.
